lessons.title: Talking and listening at work
lessons.html:
Why good talking matters at work

Every day at the abattoir, the grain silo or the poultry plant, you talk to people. You get instructions from your supervisor. You tell a co-worker that a machine is making a strange noise. You warn someone that the floor is wet. If the message is not clear, people can get hurt, meat can be spoiled and time is lost.

Speaking clearly

  • Look at the person you are talking to.
  • Speak slowly and loud enough, but do not shout.
  • Use simple words. Say 'the conveyor belt stopped' and not 'that thing is broken'.
  • Give one message at a time.
  • Ask: 'Do you understand?' or 'Can you repeat it back to me?'

Listening well

Listening is half of communication. A good listener:

  • Stops working for a moment and looks at the speaker, if it is safe to do so.
  • Does not interrupt.
  • Asks questions when something is not clear.
  • Repeats the main point back, for example: 'So you want me to clean chiller two before lunch?'

Noise on the floor

Many workplaces are noisy. Machines, compressors and animals all make sound. When it is noisy:

  • Move closer or step to a quieter place to talk.
  • Use agreed hand signals if your team has them.
  • Never remove your hearing protection in a noisy area just to chat. Rather move away from the noise.

Remember: if you are not sure what you were told, ask again. It is better to ask twice than to make a mistake once.

lessons.title: Adapting how you speak
lessons.html:
Different people, different ways of talking

We do not talk to everyone in the same way. You speak one way to a friend at lunch and another way to the farm manager or a meat inspector. Changing the way you talk to suit the person and the situation is called adapting your communication.

Think about three things

  1. Who am I talking to? A new worker, a supervisor, a visitor, a truck driver?
  2. Why am I talking? To give an instruction, to report a problem, to ask for leave, to greet?
  3. Where am I? On a noisy slaughter floor, in the office, at a team meeting?

Examples

SituationHow to speak
Showing a new worker how to use a knife steriliserSlowly, step by step, show and tell, check that they understood
Reporting a broken scale to the supervisorShort and clear: what, where, when
Greeting a visitor or inspectorPolite, use their name or title, be respectful
Talking to a friend at breakRelaxed, everyday language

Language and respect

South African workplaces have people who speak isiZulu, isiXhosa, Sesotho, Afrikaans, English and many more languages. If someone does not understand your language, use simple words, show with your hands or ask a co-worker to help translate. Never laugh at someone's accent or language. Respect builds a strong team.

Body language

Your face, hands and the way you stand also send a message. Crossed arms and a frown can look angry, even if your words are kind. Stand calmly, keep a friendly face and nod to show you are listening.

lessons.title: Handling problems in conversations
lessons.html:
When talking gets difficult

Sometimes conversations go wrong. People misunderstand each other, or someone gets angry. You need ways to keep the conversation going and fix problems.

When you do not understand

  • Say politely: 'Sorry, can you say that again?'
  • Ask the person to speak slower or show you.
  • Repeat what you think you heard and ask if it is right.

When the other person does not understand you

  • Say it again using different, simpler words.
  • Give an example or point to the thing you mean.
  • Check by asking them to tell you what they will do.

When someone is upset

Imagine a co-worker shouts at you because the crates were not washed. Do not shout back. Instead:

  1. Stay calm and keep your voice low.
  2. Listen to the full complaint.
  3. Say what you understood: 'You are upset because the crates are still dirty.'
  4. Explain your side calmly, or say what you will do to fix it.
  5. If it does not settle, ask your supervisor to help.

Taking part in team meetings

At a toolbox talk or shift meeting, you can share ideas and raise safety concerns. Wait for your turn, speak clearly, and keep to the point. If you see a danger, always report it, even if you feel shy.

Key points

  • Speak clearly, use simple words and check that the listener understood.
  • Listen without interrupting and repeat the main point back.
  • Adapt how you speak to the person, the purpose and the place.
  • Respect other languages and accents.
  • Stay calm when there is conflict and ask your supervisor for help if needed.

quiz.question: Your supervisor gives you an instruction you did not fully hear. What should you do?

options.text: Guess what was meant and carry on
Politely ask the supervisor to repeat it
Ask a co-worker later in the day

quiz.question: What is a good way to check that a listener understood your message?

options.text: Ask them to repeat it back to you

quiz.question: You must talk to a co-worker in a very noisy area. What should you do?

options.text: Move to a quieter place or use agreed hand signals
Shout as loud as you can
Do not talk at all, even about danger

quiz.question: What does it mean to adapt your communication?

options.text: Speaking the same way to everyone
Changing how you speak to suit the person and situation

quiz.question: A co-worker shouts at you because the crates are dirty. What is the best first step?

options.text: Stay calm and listen to the full complaint
